editorial_contributions.text:
This book is intended as a handbook for students of higher technical schools of specializations like applied mathematics or informatics as well as for students of specializations with extended courses of numerical methods and computer programming. It represents a brief elaboration of extremely numerous subjects. The book includes the following sections: 
{
\parindent=6mm
\begin{itemize}
  \item[]Introduction. Basic definitions from naive set theory and abstract algebra.
  \item[I.]Modular arithmetic 
  \begin{itemize}
    \item[1.]Divisibility: prime numbers and Miller-Rabin primality test, fundamental theorem of arithmetic, the greatest common divisor, Euclid's algorithm for finding \(\operatorname{gcd}(n,m)\) and extended Euclidean algorithm, the least common multiple, continued fraction expansion of real numbers (rational and irrational cases). 
    \item[2.]Möbius and Euler functions. Functions: floor, ceiling and fractional part. Multiplicative functions, Möbius function and Möbius inverse formula. Euler phi-function. 
    \item[3.]Congruences -- basic properties, complete and the least residue systems, Euler's and Fermat's theorems, modular arithmetic -- three respective algorithms are given. 
    \item[4.]Linear congruences, Chinese remainder theorem with Gauss's proof and some generalization, integral polynomial congruences and the Chinese remainder theorem for polynomials. Kurt Hensel's theorem with application. 
    \item[5.]Quadratic residues -- basic properties. 
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[5.2]Legendre symbol with ten fundamental properties (given in very applicable manner) including Gauss's and Einstein's lemmas and the quadratic reciprocity law (for odd prime numbers). 
      \item[5.3]Jacobi symbol and the quadratic reciprocity law (for odd and relatively prime positive integers). Algorithm for computation of the Jacobi and Legendre symbols. 
      \item[5.4]Theorems on solutions for the general quadratic congruences.
    \end{itemize}
    \item[6.] Exponent, universal exponent, primitive roots of given \(m=p^{\alpha}\), \(2p^{\alpha}\), 2 and 4, indices (discrete logarithms). 
    \item[7.]Groups, rings, fields, rings \(P[x]\) of polynomials in the unknown \(x\) over the field \(P\), linear spaces, finite fields. Eleven different algorithms on fundamental aspects of this algebraic structures are presented (for example, the ones for finding the multiplicative inverses of elements of \({\mathbb{F}}_{p^m}\), the order of elements of given finite group, the Gauss algorithm). 
    \item[8.]Application of modular arithmetic to cryptography. 
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[8.1]Overview of cryptography and basic notions. Hash function and MASH algorithm. 
      \item[8.2]Factoring. Three algorithms are given -- two Pollard's algorithms: the rho algorithm and the \(p-1\) factoring algorithm and, as the third one, the quadratic sieve factoring algorithm. 
      \item[8.3]RSA problem. 
      \item[8.4]Quadratic residue problem (five algorithms are included in this section). 
      \item[8.5]Discrete logarithms problem. Three algorithms are given: Baby Step, Giant Step-Shank's algorithm, Pollard's rho algorithm and the Pohlig-Hellman algorithm. 
      \item[8.6]Subset of the sum problem (with two algorithms). 
      \item[8.7]Factorization of polynomials over finite fields. Square-free algorithm and Q-matrix Berlekamp's algorithm are discussed here. 
      \item[8.8]RSA algorithm. 
      \item[8.9]RSA signatures. 
      \item[8.10]ElGamal public key cryptosystem. 
      \item[8.11]ElGamal signature scheme. 
      \item[8.12,13]General ElGamal cryptosystem and signature scheme, respectively, with multiplicative group \(G\) of Galois field \(GF(p^m)\). 
      \item[8.14]Digital signature algorithm (DSA). 
      \item[8.15,16,17]Rabin's cryptosystem and Rabin's signature scheme. 
      \item[8.18]McEliece cryptosystem. 
      \item[8.19]Merkle-Hellman knapsack encryption scheme. 
      \item[8.20]Chor-Rivest knapsack public-key encryption scheme. 
      \item[8.21]Probabilistic public-key encryption. 
      \item[8.22,23]Goldwasser-Micali and Bloom-Goldwasser probabilistic coding schemes. 
      \item[8.24,25,26,27]Feige-Fiat-Shamir signature scheme, Guillou-Quisquater (GQ) signature scheme, Schnorr and Niberg-Ruppel signature schemes. 
    \end{itemize}
    \item[9.]Real recurrence sequences, finite differences, difference equations, linear recurrence sequences (homogenous and nonhomogenous of constant and variable coefficients): solutions, concept of the so-called Casoratian of a set of solutions, Lagrange's method of finding the special solution of nonhomogenous linear recurrence sequence. 
  \end{itemize}
  \item[II.] Combinatorics -- basic concepts. 
  \begin{itemize}
    \item[10.]Permutations and combinations, choices with repetition, addition principle, multinomial coefficients. 
    \item[11.]Generating functions (as formal power series), special generating functions for combinations, choices with constraints on repetitions and without any constraints on repetitions. 
    \item[12.]Principle of inclusion and exclusion with some applications. 
  \end{itemize}
  \item[III.]Algebra of logics and predicates. 
  \begin{itemize}
    \item[13.]Logic functions, Boolean functions, formulae, normal forms, minimized normal forms (with six algorithms), minimization of the partially defined functions (the section contains two respective algorithms), dual functions, Zegalkin's polynomial over field \(F\), Zegalkin's theorem, linear functions, monotonic functions, Post's theorem. 
    \item[14.]Functions of the \(k\)-values logic, monotonic functions (partial orders and Martyniuk's theorem), linear functions, functions preserving partition, classes of type \(C\) and \(B\). 
    \item[15.]Partially ordered sets, Zorn's lemma, lattices, isomorphisms of lattices, Boolean algebras and Stone's theorem for the finite Boolean algebras (proof of this one is included). 
    \item[16.]Logic circuits analysis. Shannon functions (complexity of the boolean minimal realization problem), Lapunov's theorem, multiplexers. 
    \item[17.]Logic of predicates, quantifiers, terms, formulae, subformulae, formulae in prenex form (theorem saying that every formula is equivalent in logic of predicates to a formula in prenex form). Church's theorem. Theorems on decidability of the existential formulae and universal formulae. 
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[17.6--10]Relations, compositions of functions, Malcev's operations over functions, algebra of relations, Post's co-algebra. 
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
  \item[IV.]Graphs and algorithms. 
  \begin{itemize}
    \item[18.]Terminology of graphs, digraphs, Dijkstra algorithm. 
    \item[19.]Eulerian circuits and graphs, De Bruijn sequences, Hamiltonian circuits and graphs, Gray codes. 
    \item[20.]Trees and forests (basic nations and facts), spanning trees of connected graphs. 
    \item[21.]Circuits in graphs, linear space of subgraphs of the given graph, subspace of even subgraphs (cycle space) and induced cycles, cyclomatic number of the given graph, Kirchhoff's matrix theorem. 
    \item[22.]Bipartite graphs. Matching in bipartite graphs: Rado's theorem (on injective choices) and Hall's theorem. 
    \item[23.]Planar graphs: Euler's formula, proofs of non-planarity of graphs \(K_5\) and \(K_{3,3}\) are presented, Kuratowski's theorem on planarity and Petersen graph, algorithm for finding a plane graph of the given planar graph. 
    \item[24.]Coloring of graphs. Chromatic number of the graph, lower and upper bounds of chromatic number, bichromatic graphs and five respective algorithms. Five color theorem (with Heawood's proof by induction). In my opinion, the comments on the four color theorem, contained in this section, is insufficient. 
    \item[25.]Networks and flows. Basic concepts and facts: capacity of the cut in flow network, \(s-t\) flow network, Ford-Fulkerson theorem. 
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[25.6]Two algorithms for maximum flow (including also Dijkstra algorithm) are presented. 
    \end{itemize}
    \item[26.]Counting graphs -- this section contains, among others, Burnside's lemma and Pólya's theorem of counting (both with proofs) and their very interesting applications to the problem of coloring of the set of vertices in the cube. 
  \end{itemize}
  \item[V.]Monadic logic and finite automata. 
  \begin{itemize}
    \item[27.]Finite automata, Mealy and Moore models of automata, regular languages and some closure properties of regular languages, minimization of finite automata. 
    \item[28.]Macroautomata. 
    \item[29.]Uniformization of finite automata languages. 
    \item[30.]Monadic logic. 
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
}
In my opinion, Nabebin exposes the subjects in a very good way and in an impressive didactic spirit. From one side he gives to the teacher, and to the student as well, a possibility of completing practically every one of the discussed subjects. From the other side the book assures a sufficient support in each of the fields presented for every reader, for the new students as well as for the experienced readers who intend to quickly refresh some forgotten subjects. 
 
In a very good way, I may even say, magnificently, the author deals with mathematical formalism. Presented proofs of selected facts are brief but also clear, like for example the proofs of theorems concerning the elementary number theory, linear recurrence sequences, Boolean algebras etc. Also examples illustrating the discussed problems (theorems, algorithms) are the right ones and reliably chosen. The algorithms (and there is really a lot of them) are explained neatly and simply and, what is interesting, they are very inspiring (while reading the various algorithms I have asked many times questions to myself about the various additional variants or I have even formulated some new problems in their context). 
 
Moreover, the author makes a lot of efforts for introducing to the reader the problems which are almost standard, but they are presented in definitely more general frame. This makes for an additional quality of the book, since it provokes the reader to discussions or possible generalizations. 
 
Summarizing, I warmly recommend the book of Nabebin. It is magnificently written by the master of didactics and the excellent mathematician. 

Remark: A comparison of the book under review with other books on discrete mathematics is very difficult, almost impossible. As a last remark I might add that the reader who is more experienced in the abstractive contents of the book can certainly more easily be convinced of its teaching quality.

editorial_contributions.text:
This volume surveys the development of combinatorics since 1930 by presenting in chronological order the fundamental results of the subject proved in the original papers. 

We begin with the celebrated theorem of \textit{F. P. Ramsey} [On a problem of formal logic, Proc. Lond. Math. Soc. (2) 30, 264--286 (1929; JFM 55.0032.04)], originally developed to settle a special case of the decision problem for the predicate calculus with equality. It remains to this day the fundamental generalization of the classical pigeonhole principle. The paper by \textit{P. Erdős} and \textit{G. Szekeres} [A combinatorial problem in geometry, Compos. Math. 2, 463--470 (1935; Zbl 0012.27010)] was one of the first applications of Ramsey's theorem, and it is still one of the most elegant. Through the partition calculus of \textit{P. Erdős} and \textit{R. Rado} [A partition calculus in ser theory, Bull. Am. Math. Soc. 62, 427--489 (1956; Zbl 0071.05105)], Ramsey's theorem made inroads into the set theory, where nowadays it holds the limelight. The next major advance along the lines initiated by Ramsey came with the work of \textit{A. W. Hales} and \textit{R. I. Jewett} [Regularity and positional games, Trans. Am. Math. Soc. 106, 222--229 (1963; Zbl 0113.14802)], a result which has served as a foundation for much further work in the area. The categorical underpinning of Ramsey theory was worked out by \textit{R. L. Graham}, \textit{K. Leeb} and \textit{B. L. Rothschild} [Ramsey's theorem for a class of categories, Adv. Math. 8, 417--431 (1972; Zbl 0231.05019)]. Here the original ideas of Ramsey are cleverly blended with the contribution of Hales and Jewett. 


\textit{H. Whitney}'s paper ``Non-separable and planar graphs'' [Trans. Am. Math. Soc. 34, 339--362 (1932; Zbl 0004.13103)] makes the beginning of what is now the theory of matroids. Three years later the theory makes its appearance fully clad in another paper of \textit{H. Whitney} [On the abstract properties of linear dependence, Am. J. Math. 57, 509--533 (1935; Zbl 0012.00404)] which remains the basic reference on the subject. The theory of matroids was also in the background of \textit{W. T. Tutte}'s paper ``A ring in graph theory'' [Proc. Camb. Philos. Soc. 43, 26--40 (1947; Zbl 0031.41803)]. Tutte's paper is couched in the language of graphs and was later generalized to arbitrary matroids by Brylawski. The motivation behind much of the work of the two outstanding graph theorists of the day, Whitney and Tutte, was the coloring problem for graphs. Two short and elegant results on coloring problems are \textit{R. L. Brook}'s theorem [On colouring the nodes of a network, Proc. Camb. Philos. Soc. 37, 194--197 (1941; Zbl 0027.26403)] relating the chromatic number of a graph to its maximal degree and \textit{L. Lovasz}'s theorem [A characterization of perfect graphs, J. Comb. Theory, Ser. B 13, 95--98 (1972; Zbl 0241.05107)] characterizing perfect graphs. 


\textit{Philip Hall}'s paper ``On representatives of subsets'' [J. Lond. Math. Soc. 10, 26--30 (1935; Zbl 0010.34503)] was the first in what is now called matching theory. A very short proof of Hall's marriage theorem was given by \textit{P. R. Halmos} and \textit{H. E. Vaughan} [The marriage problem, Am. J. Math. 72, 214--215 (1950; Zbl 0034.29601)]. In the same year \textit{R. P. Dilworth} [A decomposition theorem for partially ordered sets, Ann. Math. (2) 51, 161--166 (1950; Zbl 0038.02003)] proved his famous decomposition theorem for partially ordered sets, which generalizes Hall's theorem. Several other minimax combinatorial theorems can be viewed as variants or generalizations of the marriage theorem. Such are \textit{W. T. Tutte}'s definitive work on factors in graphs [The factors of graphs, Can. J. Math. 4, 314--328 (1952; Zbl 0049.24202)], \textit{L. R. Ford} and \textit{D. R. Fulkerson}'s theory of flow in networks [Maximal flow through a network, Can. J. Math. 8, 399--404 (1956; Zbl 0073.40203)], and \textit{J. Edmonds}'s efficient algorithm for matching in graphs [Paths, trees, and flowers, Can. J. Math. 17, 449--467 (1965; Zbl 0132.20903)]. \textit{D. Gale} [A theorem on flows in networks, Pac. J. Math. 7, 1073--1082 (1957; Zbl 0087.16303)] used network flow theory to prove a result on matrices of 0's and 1's with given row and column sums also proved directly by \textit{H. J. Ryser} [Combinatorial properties of matrices of zeros and ones, Can. J. Math. 9, 371--377 (1957; Zbl 0079.01102)]. 


\textit{N. G. de Bruijn} and \textit{T. van Aardenne-Ehrenfest} [Circuits and trees in oriented linear graphs, Simon Stevin 28, 203--217 (1951; Zbl 0044.38201)], taking their lead for the early work of Kirchhoff, obtained a definitive result, now called the BEST theorem (de Bruijn-Ehrenfest-Stone-Tutte) concerning the enumeration of spanning trees and Eulerian circuits of a graph by determinants. Several years later, \textit{P. W. Kasteleyn} [The statistics of dimers on a lattice. I: The number of dimer arrangements on a quadratic lattice, Physica 27, 1209--1225 (1961; Zbl 1244.82014)] succeeded in solving a packing problem for dimers on lattice by reducing the problem to the evaluation of Pfaffians. 


\textit{G. Pólya}'s paper on picture-writing [On picture-writing, Am. Math. Mon. 63, 689--697 (1956; Zbl 0074.25005)] foreshadows the notion of the incidence algebra, a term introduced years later by \textit{G.-C. Rota} [On the foundations of combinatorial theory. I: Theory of Möbius functions, Z. Wahrscheinlichkeitstheor. Verw. Geb. 2, 340--368 (1964; Zbl 0121.02406)] in his theory of Möbius functions. Rota's work as substantially extended by \textit{H. H. Crapo} [Möbius inversion in lattices, Arch. Math. 19, 595--607 (1968; Zbl 0208.29303)]. The mystery of the characteristic polynomial, defined in terms of the Möbius function of a partially ordered set, motivates \textit{R. P. Stanley}'s beautiful result [Acyclic orientations of graphs, Discrete Math. 5, 171--178 (1973; Zbl 0258.05113)] on acyclic orientations of graphs. \textit{L. Geissinger}'s three papers [Valuations on distributive lattices. I--III. Arch. Math. 24, 230--239 (1973), 24, 337--345 (1973), 24, 475--481 (1973; Zbl 0268.06008)] are the definitive presentation of the theory of Möbius functions. 


The subject that is now called extremal set theory is represented by \textit{G. Katona}'s paper [A theorem of finite sets, Proc. Colloq. Tihany, Hungary, Sept. 1966, 187--207 (1968; Zbl 0313.05003)]. The main result, independently proved by Kruskal, harks back to a theorem of Macaulay, and was generalized by \textit{G. F. Clements} and \textit{B. Lindström} [A generalization of a combinatorial theorem of Macaulay, J. Comb. Theory 7, 230--238 (1969; Zbl 0186.01704)]. \textit{D. Lubell}'s blitz proof of Sperner's theorem [A short proof of Sperner's lemma, J. Comb. Theory 1, 299 (1966; Zbl 0151.01503)] has been extensively generalized and applied to many problems. \textit{D. J. Kleitman}'s solution [On a lemma of Littlewood and Offord on the distributions of linear combinations of vectors, Adv. Math. 5, 155--157 (1970; Zbl 0195.40703)] of a long-standing problem of Erdős related to the Littlewood/Offord problem shows the power of a simple, but far from obvious, induction argument. 


\textit{R. L. Brooks}, \textit{C. A. B. Smith}, \textit{A. H. Stone} and \textit{W. T. Tutte}'s paper [The dissection of rectangles into squares, Duke Math. J. 7, 312--340 (1940; Zbl 0024.16501)] on the decomposition of rectangles into squares was the first to use Kirchhoff's laws for the solution of a problem in combinatorics, a technique that has since become standard. 


\textit{I. Kaplansky}'s solution [Solution of the ``problème des ménages'', Bull. Am. Math. Soc. 49, 784--785 (1943; Zbl 0060.02904)] of the problème des ménages using the inclusion-exclusion principle has developed into what is now the theory of permutations with restricted position. \textit{L. Lovasz}'s contribution [A note on the line reconstruction problem, J. Comb. Theory, Ser. B 13, 309--310 (1972; Zbl 0244.05012)] to the Ulam reconstruction problem is another ingenious use of the inclusion-exclusion principle. 


\textit{P. Erdős}'s paper on graph theory and probability [Graph theory and probability, Can. J. Math. 11, 34--38 (1959; Zbl 0084.39602)] is the first paper to show how probabilistic methods can lead to combinatorial existence theorems. A substantial number of theorems in combinatorics, for which no explicit construction is known, can be given existence proofs by this method. 


\textit{C. Schensted}'s bijection [Longest increasing and decreasing subsequences, Can. J. Math. 13, 179--191 (1961; Zbl 0097.25202)] between permutations and pairs of standard Young diagrams has proved central in the seemingly unrelated topics of plane partitions and representations of the symmetric group. \textit{M. P. Schützenberger}'s paper [On a theorem of R. Jungen, Proc. Am. Math. Soc. 13, 885--890 (1962; Zbl 0107.03103)] lays the foundation of what is now the theory of rational and algebraic power series in noncommutative variables. \textit{C. St. J. A. Nash-Williams}'s striking proof [On well-quasi-ordering finite trees, Proc. Camb. Philos. Soc. 59, 833--835 (1963; Zbl 0122.25001)] that finite trees form a well- quasi-ordered set has blossomed both in logic and in graph theory. \textit{I. J. Good}'s short proof [Short proof of a conjecture by Dyson, J. Math. Phys. 11, 1884 (1970)] of a conjecture of Dyson has since been widely generalized but his approach is still the good one.
